As other have alluded to the primary difference between Ubuntu and Mint is just default configuration. Nothing really stops you from configuring one to look and act like the other. That being said it's always nice to start with a default configuration that most closely matches what you want in the end. The biggest difference in configuration is the choice of default desktop environment. If you like Unity, use Ubuntu, if you like Cinnamon use Mint, if you like KDE use Kubuntu, etc... As long as you stick with the most recent LTS release you'll get a good mix of stability, and up to date packages.

As for using Debian directly, I'd recommend against it. Debian Stable releases come around every two years or so just like *buntu LTS releases, however the release process in Debian means that you won't have the newest version of anything. However, like the name implies it's rock solid stable. On a server, I really like using Debian Stable. Many people run the "Testing" release of Debian, which is more up to date then the stable release but still behind the *buntus. Despite the name "Testing" is pretty stable. Yet other people run the "Unstable" release of Debian which is what the *buntus are based on. This gives you up to date packages, but not much of a guarantee of stability. The *buntus give you all the benefits of running Debian unstable but with some testing to make sure things don't break.

Beyond the stability and configuration stuff, the other difference between the *buntus and Debian is "freedom". Given a choice between anything and freedom, Debian picks freedom every time. This is great from a philosophy standpoint, and it's a big part of the reason why Debian is such a great base to build on, but it does mean that in cases where there was a choice between ease of use and freedom, Debian went with freedom.
